name: FOL-005

lead: FOL-005 is a short peptide derived from osteopontin, a protein found in hair follicles. It was developed by Follicum, and is sometimes mentioned in hair-loss discussions because it acts on the hair growth cycle.

Lab work published in 2020 found that it pushed human hair follicles toward the resting phase, which was framed as a possible treatment for unwanted hair rather than for thinning. A related analogue has been studied for blood-vessel repair. Published human hair-regrowth results were not found.

paras: FOL-005 is a research peptide and not an approved cosmetic. Published formulation work has looked at delivering it into the skin through a topical microparticle preparation.
It has no approved medical use, so no label safety information exists. Laboratory studies reported no signs of toxicity in the models used, but human safety data for hair use are not published.

angle.text: The appeal for appearance is the idea that a peptide could modulate the hair cycle. Published laboratory work shows effects on follicle cycling and a mechanism involving neuropilin-1; human appearance outcomes have not been published.

lead: FOL-005 is a modified peptide fragment derived from osteopontin, a multifunctional glycoprotein that human hair follicles express.[1] It is discussed in hair-focused communities as a peptide that acts on follicle biology, which could in principle influence how much hair a person keeps.

In a 2020 study using cultured human follicles and scalp skin transplanted onto mice, FOL-005 pushed follicles toward the catagen (regression) phase and lowered production of fibroblast growth factor-7, without reducing follicle stem cells.[1] The authors framed this as a route to treatments for unwanted hair growth. A 2024 paper reported that FOL-005 stimulated hair growth in the context of studying its receptor, neuropilin-1, using a more stable analogue called FOL-026.[2]

paras: FOL-005 was identified as a modified osteopontin fragment that binds to the hair follicle.[1] In follicle culture it reduced expression of FGF7, a hair growth promoter, and adding recombinant FGF7 partly reversed the catagen effect.[1]

A 2024 study used glyco-capture technology to identify neuropilin-1, a co-receptor for VEGF receptors, as the likely receptor for FOL-005 and the more stable FOL-026. FOL-026 activated VEGFR-2 signalling, promoted endothelial cell growth and migration, and stimulated angiogenesis in animal models.[2]
A 2022 pharmaceutical study developed a water-free microparticle formulation intended to deliver FOL-005 into skin and follicles while keeping the peptide stable.[3]
No studies found. Published work to date consists of ex vivo human follicle experiments, animal xenograft models, receptor studies and formulation development.[1][2][3]
Discussion is limited; the peptide appears in lists of experimental hair compounds.

timeline.event: Study reports FOL-005 promotes catagen in human follicles.[1]
